sentences.text: All species of Arthropterygius grew to lengths between 3 and 5 meters.
The animal possessed a very short but robust snout relative to its total skull length.
Its eye socket measured about 0.34 times the length of the skull.
Arthropterygius had a pineal foramen that was proportionately larger than in any other known ophthalmosaurid.
The genus Arthropterygius was formally described by Maxwell in 2010.
Fossils of this creature have been found in Canada, Norway, Russia, and Argentina.
These remains represent the most complete ichthyosaur fossils discovered in the Canadian Arctic.
In 2012, a skull and forefin of an ophthalmosaurid ichthyosaur were described from the Neuquén Basin in Argentina.
Arthropterygius chrisorum is designated as the type species of the genus.
Fossils of A. chrisorum, A. lundi, and A. hoybergeti originate from the Slottsmøya Member of the Agardhfjellet Formation.
The seafloor at this site lay approximately 150 meters below the surface in relatively oxygen-poor waters.
Researchers suggest that sea ice was likely present during winter due to the location's high latitude and the cool Tithonian climate.
The Slottsmøya Member also contains fossils of other marine reptiles such as Undorosaurus gorodischensis, Nannopterygius borealis, and Brachypterygius sp.
This formation includes 21 plesiosaurian specimens, with Pliosaurus funkei likely serving as the apex predator.
Maxwell (2010) classified Arthropterygius as the sister taxon to the Argentine ophthalmosaurid Caypullisaurus.
Many recent cladistic analyses instead classify Arthropterygius as the basalmost member of the family Ophthalmosauridae.
Ophthalmosaurus chrisorum is considered a synonym of Arthropterygius chrisorum.
Arthropterygius fossils date from the Kimmeridgian to possibly the Berriasian.
The animal lived during the late Jurassic and possibly into the earliest Cretaceous.
It lived from the Oxfordian to the Tithonian stages, between 161.5 and 143.1 million years ago.
The geological outcrops in Svalbard containing Arthropterygius fossils date to the Volgian stage, roughly corresponding to the Tithonian-early Berriasian.
It is debated whether the large pineal foramen in Arthropterygius was an adaptation to high-latitude environments.
It is debated whether Janusaurus, Keilhauia, and Palvennia should be treated as synonyms of Arthropterygius, as some studies suggest the evidence does not support this synonymy.
